source.title_on_document: FIERO: Empowering Creative Writing Through Collaborative Game Play

supplement.where: Appendices A-H, pp. 41-51 of this PDF. Appendix H (p. 51) points to https://github.com/zxioke/FAIero-game for system, card, and prompt artifacts; no separate statistical supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: Appendix A, Tables 1-2 (pp. 41-42), contains self-report questionnaire means, SDs, group counts, Mann-Whitney z statistics, p values, and effect sizes r. Appendix B (p. 42) gives interview questions; C (pp. 42-44), participant demographics; D (pp. 44-47), the story-evaluation rubric and prompt; E (pp. 47-48), participant instructions; F (pp. 48-50, including Table 5 on p. 49), models, decoding parameters, and prompts; G (pp. 50-51), conflict resolution; H (p. 51), the artifact release. The scored-story percentages and overall chi-squared tests are in the main text and Figures 13-14 (pp. 27-29). No participant- or team-level SEs or CIs for the scored-story outcomes are supplied.

paper_design_summary: In an offline, between-subjects experiment, 60 people were randomly assigned to FIERO or Google Docs collaborative writing and worked face to face in teams of three on a superhero story (pp. 13-16, Sections 4.1-4.4). FIERO combined physical cards and a game interface with generative-AI imagery, decision support, and story refinement, with AI available during production of the final stories (pp. 12-14; p. 48, Appendix E.2). Three LLM judges compared final stories on seven dimensions; questionnaires were analyzed for 60 people, but content analysis reports nine texts per arm despite ten teams per arm being reported, and does not state the number of people represented by the scored texts (pp. 16-17, 27-29, 41-44).

studies.label: FIERO versus Google Docs collaborative superhero-story writing

assignment.what_was_assigned: The paper states that participants were randomly assigned to FIERO or Google Docs story creation and were organized into groups of three. Individual is the stated assignment unit, but the randomization procedure and timing of team formation relative to allocation are not explained (p. 13, Section 4.1). The assigned FIERO condition combines AI with physical cards and the game interface (pp. 13-14, Section 4.1; p. 34, Section 6.6.1).
assignment.quote: In this between-subjects experiment, 60 participants were randomly assigned to either a story creation group or a card game-based story creation group.
assignment.locator: p. 13, Section 4.1, Study Design; pp. 13-14, condition descriptions.

arms.name: FIERO
arms.description: Face-to-face teams use FIERO, physical narrative cards, generated images, optional AI decision suggestions, and final-story assistance. Both arms follow the same narrative tasks and round timing (pp. 13-14, Section 4.1; p. 48, Appendix E.2). n_analyzed is the questionnaire count of 30 (p. 41, Table 1); content analysis uses nine texts (p. 17, Section 4.5.2). Arm-specific counts at randomization are not separately reported.

arms.name: Control (Google Docs)
arms.description: Face-to-face teams use a shared Google Docs page for individual drafts, mutual review, oral discussion, and story integration. The baseline has no AI or physical cards, with human collaboration present in both arms (pp. 13-14, Section 4.1; p. 34, Section 6.6.1; pp. 47-48, Appendix E.1). n_analyzed is the questionnaire count of 30 (p. 41, Table 1); content analysis uses nine texts (p. 17, Section 4.5.2). Arm-specific counts at randomization are not separately reported.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusion procedure or attrition count is reported. The 60 analyzed people refer to questionnaire analyses: N=60 in Section 4.5.1 (p. 17) and n=30 per arm in Tables 1-2 (pp. 41-42). Recruitment reports ten teams of three per arm (p. 16, Section 4.4), whereas content analysis uses nine texts per arm (p. 17, Section 4.5.2). Omitted teams or texts are not identified and the discrepancy is not explained. The number of people represented by the scored-story subset is not stated and is unknown; no people count is inferred from texts or pairs. The questionnaire counts are retained as explicitly reported. The people checker also identified an unresolved item-denominator inconsistency: the first CSI item means in Table 2, 6.15 and 6.19, cannot be rounded means of 30 unweighted integer responses on the stated seven-point scale (p. 14, Section 4.2.1; p. 41, Table 2). Missingness, weighting, or other response processing is not explained; this does not establish a replacement analyzed people count.
participants.who: Non-professional creators interested in collaborative creative writing but not considering themselves proficient, recruited through word of mouth and social media, aged 18-28. Section 4.4 reports 80% students and 20% non-students in technology, design, media production, marketing, and administrative office work. It states that none had professional publishing or screenwriting backgrounds or prior creative-writing experience (p. 16, Section 4.4; pp. 42-44, Appendix C).
participants.quote: We recruited 30 participants for each of the Control and FIERO groups (divided into 10 teams of 3 members each) to take part in an offline collaborative writing activity.
participants.locator: p. 13, Section 4.1 (60 randomized); p. 16, Section 4.4 (recruitment and population); p. 17, Sections 4.5.1-4.5.2 (questionnaire N and nine texts per arm); pp. 41-42, Tables 1-2 (30 questionnaire participants per arm); pp. 42-44, Appendix C and Tables 3-4 (participant roster).

ai_tool.name_model: FIERO: GPT-4 for decision support and final-story assistance; GPT-4o image model (gpt-4o-image) for images (p. 12, Section 3.4; p. 49, Table 5). Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT-5.2 are post-hoc evaluators, not the assistance provided to participants (p. 17, Section 4.5.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Integrated assistance combines image generation from cards and player-authored text, context-sensitive selection among player-authored villain and weapon drafts with explanations, final narrative suggestions, and full-text polishing. Participants can accept, modify, or ignore the suggestions; assistance remains available while completing the scored final story (p. 12, Sections 3.3.3-3.4; p. 48, Appendix E.2; pp. 49-51, Appendices F-G). Coded other because these functions span image generation, decision support, and refinement; the paper does not establish refinement as the single main role.

task.description: Teams of three collaboratively create a superhero story: individual hero/backstory creation, villain and scene development, weapon and climax development, and integration into a complete story (p. 13, Section 4.1; pp. 47-48, Appendix E).
task.duration: 30 minutes as stated in Section 4.1: three rounds, each with 5 minutes of individual thinking and 5 minutes of group discussion (p. 13). Appendix E (p. 48) lists final synthesis after those rounds but gives no separate duration; no extra minutes are inferred.

outcomes.name: Creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The Creativity rubric assesses originality, innovative concepts, uniqueness, fresh perspectives, and imaginative content (pp. 15-16, Section 4.2.2; p. 46, Appendix D). Final team-written stories were judged pairwise by Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT-5.2, retained as evaluator variants of one outcome. Each of nine FIERO texts was compared with each of nine control texts in both AB and BA orders; inconsistent decisions became draws (p. 17, Section 4.5.2). n_units=81 distinct story pairs per judge, not people or independent teams (p. 27, Section 5.4.1). Figure 14 reports percentage net advantage of FIERO over control (p. 29). The paper supplies no participant- or team-adjusted SE or CI and no dimension-specific inferential test.

contrasts.reported: Net advantage (FIERO over control): Claude -27.2%; Gemini 50.6%; GPT-5.2 -7.4%.
contrasts.locator: p. 28, Section 5.4.2, Creativity; p. 29, Figure 14 and caption.

outcomes.name: Overall Preference / overall comparison
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Overall Preference assesses story quality, engagement, enjoyment, completeness, and coherence (p. 16, Section 4.2.2; p. 46, Appendix D). Section 5.4.1/Figure 13 reports overall win/loss/draw results and chi-squared tests; Figure 14 reports the Overall dimension's net advantages. Appendix D has separate Overall and Final_Winner fields (p. 47), but the paper does not map them to the two figures. Both summaries are retained here with distinct labels; they are not treated as independent outcomes or assumed equivalent. The Claude summaries do not reconcile as the same win-minus-loss measure. Chi-squared tests apply only to the Section 5.4.1 summary; adjustment for repeated use of stories is not described. Final team-written stories were judged pairwise by Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT-5.2, retained as evaluator variants of one outcome. Each of nine FIERO texts was compared with each of nine control texts in both AB and BA orders; inconsistent decisions became draws (p. 17, Section 4.5.2). n_units=81 distinct story pairs per judge, not people or independent teams (p. 27, Section 5.4.1). Figure 14 reports percentage net advantage of FIERO over control (p. 29). The paper supplies no participant- or team-adjusted SE or CI and no dimension-specific inferential test.

contrasts.reported: Overall Preference dimension (Figure 14), net advantage of FIERO over control: Claude 45.7%; Gemini 54.3%; GPT-5.2 65.4%. Separately, overall comparison (Section 5.4.1/Figure 13): FIERO win rates Claude 60.5% (49/81), Gemini 56.8% (46/81), GPT-5.2 76.5% (62/81); control win rates Claude 19.8%, Gemini 2.5%, GPT-5.2 11.1%; draws Claude 19.8%, Gemini 40.7%, GPT-5.2 12.3%. Reported chi-squared tests: Claude χ² = 16.00, p < .001; Gemini χ² = 38.35, p < .001; GPT-5.2 χ² = 39.56, p < .001.
contrasts.locator: p. 27, Section 5.4.1 and Figure 13 (overall win/loss/draw results and tests); p. 29, Section 5.4.2, Overall, and Figure 14, Overall row (dimension net advantages); p. 47, Appendix D (output fields).

eligibility.reason: All three criteria are met for S1 under the current study-level rule. The paper explicitly states that 60 participants were randomly assigned to the two collaborative story-creation conditions (p. 13, Section 4.1). FIERO provided GPT-4 text assistance and GPT-4o image generation during creation of the scored final stories; the comparison used Google Docs without AI (p. 12, Sections 3.3.3-3.4; pp. 13-14, Section 4.1; p. 34, Section 6.6.1; p. 48, Appendix E.2; p. 49, Table 5). Criterion 2 uses the explicitly reported analyzed sample for this study: questionnaire N=60 and n=30 per arm (p. 17, Section 4.5.1; p. 41, Table 1). The questionnaire item means do not independently validate those denominators; their arithmetic inconsistency does not establish a smaller replacement N (p. 14, Section 4.2.1; p. 41, Table 2). Final participant-produced stories were scored for creativity and other narrative qualities by LLM judges, satisfying criterion 3 (pp. 15-17, Sections 4.2.2 and 4.5.2; pp. 27-29, Section 5.4; pp. 44-47, Appendix D). The nine analyzed texts per arm have no explicitly reported participant headcount or explanation of omitted texts; neither the study-level N=60 nor the 81 story pairs is assigned as the participant N for these estimates (p. 17, Section 4.5.2; p. 27, Section 5.4.1). AI is bundled with physical cards and the game interface, and the reported tests supply no participant- or team-adjusted precision. These limitations affect interpretation and later extraction, without overturning the three study-level eligibility criteria.

one_line_finding: Creativity judgments of FIERO's bundled card-game/AI condition differed by evaluator (net advantage: Claude -27.2%, Gemini 50.6%, GPT-5.2 -7.4%), while overall-preference net advantages favored FIERO (45.7-65.4%; p. 29, Figure 14).
open_questions: Why were nine texts per arm compared when ten teams per arm were recruited, which texts or teams were omitted, and how many people are represented in the scored-story analysis (p. 16, Section 4.4; p. 17, Section 4.5.2; pp. 43-44, Tables 3-4)?
How was random assignment implemented, and how did team formation relate to allocation? Participant randomization is explicitly stated but those procedures are not described (pp. 13-14, Section 4.1).

Do Section 5.4.1/Figure 13 and the Overall row in Figure 14 represent distinct Overall/Final_Winner outputs or a reporting error? The mapping is unstated and Claude's summaries are inconsistent as the same win-minus-loss metric (pp. 27, 29; p. 47, Appendix D).

Are story-level judgments and team identifiers available to estimate uncertainty accounting for repeated use of the same stories? No participant- or team-adjusted SEs or CIs are supplied, and Appendix H does not explicitly identify a participant/story dataset (pp. 17, 27-29, 51).

What item-level denominators or response processing explain Table 2 reporting n=30 per arm alongside first-item means of 6.15 and 6.19, which cannot be rounded means of 30 unweighted integer responses on the stated seven-point scale? The paper does not explain missingness or processing, and no alternative people count can be confirmed (p. 14, Section 4.2.1; p. 41, Table 2).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-09 from both parseable raw forms and the source on file. Read every line of the markdown, including references and Appendices A-H; verified coded facts and all recorded numbers against PDF text and inspected the printed labels of Figures 13-14 using in-memory PDF renders. PDF and printed pagination coincide. No effect sizes, inferred participant counts, or other unprinted statistics were calculated. Both screeners list the same seven scored-story outcomes with the same constructs, questions, units, AI availability, timing, primary status, and substantive result directions. The two substantive A/B differences are the AI-role code and the overall-comparison statistics-availability list. Equivalent wording, expanded locators, empty versus not_stated country coding, and compatible descriptive additions are not counted as differences. B's damaged minus signs are restored from the PDF; its accompanying statement already identifies Claude and GPT-5.2 as favoring control, so this is an encoding correction rather than a different finding. The damaged chi-squared symbol in both raw forms is also corrected. Compatible details from both forms, including the reported population breakdown and the final-synthesis timing caveat, are retained. No outcome is explicitly designated primary. Overall comparison and Overall Preference remain one outcome with separate summaries and their unresolved relationship stated. CSI, CSE, and SSA questionnaires measure participant perceptions and are not eligible output scores; the abstract's idea-fluency and novelty-generation claims concern these self-reports (pp. 14-15, Section 4.2.1; pp. 41-42, Tables 1-2). The qualitative examples of stereotypes, narrative changes, and homogenization supply no quantitative diversity outcome across people; no unassisted after-AI task is reported. Human experts helped define the judging rubric but did not directly score the final judgments (p. 17, Section 4.5.2; p. 35, Section 6.6.8). Appendix G describes design and grounding rather than a separate scored creativity study (pp. 50-51). No preregistration, shared participant sample, or reanalysis of another paper is stated; absence of a sample-sharing statement is not proof of no overlap. Participant country is not stated and has not been inferred from affiliations. The repository URL identifies code/cards/prompts; no explicit participant/story data URL is supplied (p. 51, Appendix H). The count of 60 is confirmed only for the study's questionnaire analysis, not for scored-story participants. n_unresolved counts unresolved A/B differences; shared source-reporting gaps remain in open_questions and are not counted as disagreements. Finalized on 2026-10-09 after independently reading all 1,412 markdown lines, including references and Appendices A-H, extracting the relevant PDF pages with PyMuPDF, and inspecting Figures 13-14 through in-memory PDF renders. The assignment, outcome, and people challenge files each contain an empty problems list, so challenge_resolution is empty and all three challenge-resolution counts are zero. Their substantive confirmations were checked against the source. The people checker's questionnaire-denominator caveat was independently confirmed and added to participants.exclusions and open_questions; no alternative sample size was inferred. The existing supplement description and lab_rct classification conform to the current spec, and this is not a reanalysis of another paper. Analysis-count prose uses analyzed. Each open question has a resolution route in final.open_items; none changes eligibility under the current study-level analyzed-N rule. Both reconciliation differences were already resolved, and the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged.

open_items.item: Scored-story sample and exclusions: authors need to identify which texts or teams were omitted and link the nine analyzed texts per arm to participants (p. 16, Section 4.4; p. 17, Section 4.5.2; pp. 43-44, Tables 3-4). This affects estimate-level participant counts, but not criterion 2 under the current study-level rule: questionnaire analyses explicitly report N=60 (p. 17, Section 4.5.1; p. 41, Table 1).

Randomization implementation and timing of team formation: authors need to describe the allocation method and whether teams were formed before or after allocation. This does not leave criterion 1 unclear because random assignment of participants is explicitly stated (p. 13, Section 4.1).

Relationship between the overall comparison in Section 5.4.1/Figure 13 and the Overall row in Figure 14: authors need to map Overall and Final_Winner to the reported summaries or correct a reporting error (pp. 27, 29; p. 47, Appendix D). This affects extraction of the overall result, not any eligibility criterion; the creativity outcome remains an output score.

Uncertainty accounting for repeated story use: posted story-level judgments with story and team identifiers would permit an analysis that respects the dependence among comparisons (p. 17, Section 4.5.2; pp. 27-29, Section 5.4). Appendix H identifies artifacts but no explicit participant/story dataset (p. 51). This affects precision and pooling, not the three eligibility criteria.

Questionnaire item denominators and processing: authors need to explain the first-item means of 6.15 and 6.19 despite n=30 per arm on a seven-point integer scale (p. 14, Section 4.2.1; p. 41, Table 2). This is a reporting-validation gap and does not establish that the explicitly reported study-level analyzed N=60 is below the eligibility threshold; no replacement N is inferred.
